title: Question 7
stem:
The circuit for an inverting amplifier incorporating an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp) is shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: explain why point $P$ is known as a virtual earth

markscheme_points.text: for amplifier not to saturate, V+ = V– or feedback (loop) ensures V+ = V–
V+ is at earth/0 V so V– is (almost) at earth/0 V

hints: Hint 1: Start by looking at where the two op-amp inputs are connected - what is the potential at the non-inverting (+) input in Fig. 7.1?
Hint 2: Recall that an ideal op-amp has a very large open-loop gain, so for a finite output voltage the voltage difference between the - and + inputs must be almost zero.
Hint 3: Think about why point P is at earth potential but is not actually wired to earth, and why almost no current enters the op-amp itself.
parts.proper_answer: The non-inverting input is earthed at $0\text{ V}$. For an ideal op-amp the potential difference between inputs is zero, so P is also at $0\text{ V}$. P is not directly connected to earth, so it is a virtual earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the earthed input**
You are sitting beside the circuit, so first check the + input. It is wired straight to the earth line, so $V_{+} = 0\text{ V}$. That is a real earth.

Step 2: **Use the golden rule for an ideal op-amp**
An ideal op-amp has huge open-loop gain $A_0$, with $$V_{OUT} = A_0(V_{+} - V_{-})$$ For $V_{OUT}$ to stay finite and not saturated, $(V_{+} - V_{-})$ must be essentially zero. So $V_{-} \approx V_{+}$.

Step 3: **Explain virtual earth**
Since $V_{+} = 0\text{ V}$, point P at the - input is also held at about $0\text{ V}$. It behaves like earth in potential, but there is no wire from P to earth and no current flows into the op-amp input. That is why it is called a virtual earth, not a real earth.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: calculate the gain of the amplifier.
hints: Hint 1: Identify this as an inverting amplifier and recall which two resistors set the magnitude of the voltage gain.
Hint 2: Remember to include the minus sign for phase inversion and check the ratio of the $5.2\text{ k}\Omega$ feedback resistor to the $0.80\text{ k}\Omega$ input resistor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the inverting gain rule**
For an inverting amplifier with virtual earth at P, all the input current flows through the feedback resistor. This gives $$G = \frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}$$ The minus sign means the output is inverted relative to the input.

Step 2: **Put in the numbers**
Here $R_f = 5.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{in} = 0.80\text{ k}\Omega$, so $$G = -\frac{5.2}{0.80} = -6.5$$ No units, because gain is a voltage ratio.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
When the op-amp is saturated, the potential difference across the LED is $2.3\text{ V}$.

Calculate the minimum resistance of resistor $R$ so that the current in the LED is limited to $30\text{ mA}$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the output branch - the resistor R and LED D are in series across $V_{OUT}$ to earth, so think about what $V_{OUT}$ is when the op-amp saturates.
Hint 2: Use the LED voltage of $2.3\text{ V}$ to work out how much voltage must be left across resistor R, and convert the $30\text{ mA}$ limit to amperes.
Hint 3: Apply $R = V/I$ to resistor R, or treat R and the LED as a potential divider of the saturated output voltage.
parts.proper_answer: Saturated $V_{OUT} = 5\text{ V}$, p.d. across R $= 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ V}$. $R = 2.7/0.030 = 90\,\Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the saturated output voltage**
The op-amp is powered by $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$ rails. When saturated positive, $V_{OUT}$ is approximately the positive rail, so $$V_{OUT} \approx +5.0\text{ V}$$ This $5.0\text{ V}$ appears across the series combination of R and the LED to earth.

Step 2: **Share the voltage between R and LED**
The LED takes $2.3\text{ V}$, so by Kirchhoff's voltage law the resistor must drop the rest: $$V_R = V_{OUT} - V_{LED} = 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ V}$$ The same current flows through both, limited to $$I = 30\text{ mA} = 0.030\text{ A}$$

Step 3: **Calculate the minimum R**
Use Ohm's law for the resistor: $$R = \frac{V_R}{I} = \frac{2.7}{0.030} = 90\,\Omega$$ This can also be seen as an effective LED resistance of $2.3/0.030 = 77\,\Omega$ forming a divider: $2.3 = 77/(R+77) \times 5.0$. A smaller R would let more than $30\text{ mA}$ flow, so $90\,\Omega$ is the minimum safe value.
